claims.text: Actively learned moment-tensor potentials can be parameterized with ab initio data for multicomponent alloys.
A minimal, adaptively sampled set of ab initio molecular-dynamics snapshots is sufficient to train an MLIP for both solid and liquid states near melting.
The trained MLIP can replace full ab initio molecular dynamics in solid- and liquid-phase free-energy evaluations.
Representative disordered configurations, potentially including special quasirandom structures, capture the vibrational modes and electronic environments needed for accurate free energies.
Training on curated ab initio snapshots allows the MLIP to predict the complex potential-energy surface accurately.
The MLIP surrogate enables efficient phase-free-energy calculations through thermodynamic integration or related methods.
MLIP-accelerated free-energy calculations retain vibrational entropy and anharmonic contributions in both solid and liquid phases.
MLIP-accelerated free-energy calculations retain electron-vibration coupling.
The proposed workflow substantially reduces computational cost for multicomponent high-temperature systems relative to explicit ab initio molecular dynamics.
The proposed workflow will outperform TOR-TILD when applied to multicomponent systems.
The computational-cost reduction relative to full ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows will be approximately five- to tenfold.
MLIP-derived phase free energies and fusion observables will have fidelity comparable to full ab initio molecular dynamics.
The method is applicable from binary systems through multicomponent alloys containing up to five principal elements near melting.
Extreme anharmonicity, rare configurations, or incomplete coverage of electronic environments may reduce MLIP accuracy.
The workflow's performance is sensitive to the quality and representativeness of its ab initio training data.
A direct comparison of solid and liquid free energies, melting temperature, vibrational density of states, and entropy contributions against explicit ab initio calculations can test the method.
A deviation exceeding approximately 5% in MLIP-derived free energies or melting temperature relative to explicit ab initio results falsifies the hypothesis.
